opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's mostly about removing friction. I think one of the biggest mistakes people make with LLMs is that they write these short, lazy prompts in the moment, because typing out a really good, detailed prompt every time is annoying. But the quality difference between a throwaway prompt and a carefully crafted one can be enormous. So the question becomes: how do you get the benefits of the elaborate prompt without paying the cost every single time?

Text-snippet apps solve that really neatly. I have a bunch of prompts I've iterated on over time. One for giving me brutally honest feedback on a draft, one for explaining a paper at the right level of detail, one for brainstorming, and so on. Each of them is mapped to a short trigger. I type a few characters and the whole multi-paragraph prompt expands in place. Then I paste in whatever I'm working on and go.

A few things I like about this. First, it means I actually use the good prompts, rather than intending to and then being lazy. Second, it encourages iteration. When a prompt is saved somewhere, you notice when it underperforms and you go back and tweak it, so it gets better over time instead of being reinvented badly each time. And third, it works everywhere. It doesn't matter which model or which interface I'm using, the snippet just expands into whatever text box I'm in.

More broadly, I think people underrate how much of getting value from these tools is just building small habits and infrastructure around them. The models are very capable, but you often have to meet them halfway with good context and clear instructions. Anything that makes doing that the default rather than an effort is worth a lot.

r001.rationale: The candidate says snippets let the speaker invoke a multi-paragraph prompt with a few keystrokes, removing the effort that leads to short prompts, so they actually use the good prompts.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, so this is one of those productivity hacks that sounds really trivial but has genuinely changed how much I get out of these models. The basic observation is that the quality of what you get from an LLM depends enormously on the prompt, and the prompts that actually work well are often long. Like, a few paragraphs. You want to say what role you want the model to play, what context it should know about you, how you want it to push back on you, what format you want the answer in, what common failure modes you want it to avoid. And if you write that out carefully once, it's great. But nobody is going to retype three paragraphs every time they open a chat window. So in practice people type one lazy sentence and then get a mediocre answer and conclude the model isn't that useful.

The text-snippet apps just remove that friction completely. You type some short trigger, like semicolon-r-e-s for "research mode" or whatever, and it expands into the full prompt you've carefully crafted. So the cost of using your best prompt drops from, you know, a minute of typing and remembering what you wanted to say down to basically zero. And when the cost is zero, you actually do it every time.

I think the deeper point is that most of the value of these tools comes from having a small number of really good, iterated-on workflows that you reuse constantly. Like, I have one for "critique this draft harshly," one for "I'm about to make a decision, interrogate my reasoning," one for "explain this paper to me assuming I know X but not Y." Each of those I've refined over many uses, because every time the model does something annoying I go and add a line to the snippet saying "don't do that." So the prompt accumulates all that learning. Whereas if you're improvising a fresh prompt each time, you lose all of it and you're starting from scratch.

And it also means you can be much more ambitious with what you put in. You can include a bunch of personal context, your background, the kinds of answers you find useful, that you'd feel silly typing out every time but that genuinely makes the output a lot better. So yeah, it's a boring recommendation, but I think a lot of people are leaving a surprising amount of value on the table because the activation energy of good prompting is just slightly too high, and this kills that problem.

r001.rationale: The response says snippets reduce the cost of using a carefully crafted prompt to nearly zero, so people actually use their best prompts every time.

astra-6.text:
Because a good prompt is often a bit of a pain to write, and you don’t want to pay that cost every time. If you have some elaborate instructions that reliably get the model to do what you want, you can save them in a text-snippet app and insert the whole thing with a few keystrokes.

For example, you might have a prompt for getting feedback on a draft that says, “Identify the weakest parts of the argument, explain why they’re weak, and suggest concrete improvements.” You can make that much more detailed, but then using it is just typing a short shortcut and pasting your draft.

The point is to reduce friction. You put effort into the prompt once, improve it as you learn what works, and then make the useful version really easy to reach for.

r001.rationale: The response says saved snippets reduce the effort of using elaborate prompts and make a useful prompt easy to reach for, communicating that people are more likely to use it.

sol-6.1.text: Because a good prompt can be quite elaborate, and you don’t want to type the whole thing out every time. A text-snippet app lets you save it behind a short shortcut, so a few keystrokes expand into the full prompt. That makes the difference between having a useful prompt somewhere in a document and actually using it routinely. You can put effort into getting it right once, then make it almost effortless to reuse.

r001.rationale: It says a shortcut expands into the saved full prompt, making reuse almost effortless and turning a prompt from something merely saved into something used routinely.
